The salt arrives before the storm. It coats the brass dials of the receiver in a pale, greasy frost that tastes of kelp and cold iron. If you live high enough on the headland, where the old lighthouse keepers used to dry their woolens against the flue, you learn to read the weather by the friction of copper against glass: a sharp, dry screech means the wind will stay south; a low, wet sigh means the fog will swallow the shoals before dark.

Arthur was seventy-one when he stopped listening for ships and began listening for the gaps between them.

The station had been decommissioned three decades prior, stripped of its heavy Fresnel lens and left to the gulls. The government took the diesel generators, the zinc batteries, and the brass logbooks with their ruled red margins, but they left the aerial masts bolted into the granite. The masts were four hundred feet of latticed steel, stayed by thick galvanized cables that hummed in the prevailing westerlies like the bass strings of an unplayed cello.

Arthur had brought his own gear up the goat path in four separate trips: two Nagra reel-to-reel recorders in their leather field cases, five boxes of quarter-inch magnetic tape, three ribbon microphones wrapped in oiled silk, and a pair of German headphones with bakelite earcups that smelled permanently of hair tonic and woodsmoke.

His neighbors in the harbor village three miles down thought he was monitoring the cod trawlers or intercepting pirate radio from the continental shelf. They were wrong. Arthur was cataloging the decay of human resonance.

Sound, Arthur liked to say to no one in particular, does not die. It merely dilutes. A door slammed in an empty house in nineteenth-century Yorkshire does not cease to exist once the vibrations settle; its acoustic energy transfers into the plaster, into the horsehair insulation, into the grain of the floorboards, and eventually radiates out into the atmosphere as microscopic, imperceptible heat. If one possessed an instrument of infinite sensitivity, one could reconstruct the entire history of human sorrow simply by taking the temperature of a brick.

He had no such instrument, so he settled for the fringe frequencies.

Every evening at four, while the kettle whistled on the cast-iron stove, Arthur turned on the high-gain preamp. He would seat himself at the deal table, pull the heavy headphones over his ears, and spin the heavy aluminum vernier dial slowly through the shortwave bands.

Mostly, there was the white hiss of cosmic background radiation—the cooled ember of the universe’s first shout, bouncing between galaxies since before the earth was mud. But beneath the hiss, caught in the ionospheric skip between the cold Atlantic and the upper atmosphere, were the strays.

A stray was not a broadcast. A broadcast had intent; it had an announcer, a sponsor, or at least a call sign repeated in Morse every fifteen minutes. Strays were accidental leakages: the carrier tone of a forgotten telemetry beacon on an abandoned oil platform; the inductive whine of a tramway line in an inland city five hundred miles away, picked up by a fluke of damp air and reflected off a thunderhead; the dead air between two automated weather stations exchanging barometric data in binary bursts that sounded like dry peas falling on tin.

On Tuesdays, he listened for the clock.

Somewhere in the interior, across two mountain ranges and a vast peat plateau, an observatory still transmitted the exact legal second via a 50-kilowatt transmitter on 4.5 megahertz. The signal was nothing more than a click—a dry, mechanical pulse generated by a pendulum swinging through an optical gate in an underground vault. For sixty years, the pendulum had cut the light once every thousand milliseconds. But the observatory had lost its funding in the nineties. The staff had retired; the grass had grown through the tarmac of the parking lot; the roof of the library had caved in under a wet snow in 2008.

Yet the solar panels on the transmitter shed remained clear, kept clean by the high winds, and the lead-acid batteries held enough charge to keep the quartz oscillator glowing.

Arthur tuned to 4.5 megahertz.

*Click.*

He looked at the second hand of his own pocket watch, laid flat on the green blotter.

*Click.*

The interval was perfect. It was the only clean thing left in the room.

*Click.*

He took a sip of tea. It was bitter, steeped too long from leaves he had dried himself on sheets of newsprint. Outside, the first squall of the evening hit the glass, rattling the lead came. The mast outside groaned—a long, descending minor third that vibrated through the floorboards and set the spoons trembling in their ceramic crock.

He reached for the grease pencil and noted the signal strength in his ledger: *4.5 MHz. 17:04 UTC. QSA 4. Heavy static from western front. Pulse remains square.*

People often asked him—when he went down to the post office on alternate Thursdays to collect his pension and two tins of tobacco—if he ever got lonely up on the point. The postmistress, a woman named Clara whose knuckles were swollen from thirty years of sorting parcels, always asked with a soft, pitying tilt of her head, as if solitude were a convalescence he was failing to complete.

"There’s too much noise for loneliness, Clara," he told her once.

She had laughed, assuming it was a joke about the gannets that nested in the cliffs below the lantern room. He hadn't corrected her. How could he explain that every square meter of the air above her village was crowded with sixty years of amateur radio chatter, lost aircraft navigation pings, the faint magnetic signatures of power grids stretching from Lisbon to Murmansk, and the lingering echoes of maritime distress calls whose vessels had long since turned into reefs?

We are not alone; we are merely deafened by the present.

Around nine o’clock, the wind backed to the northwest. The hiss in the headphones deepened, taking on the hollow, oceanic quality that meant the ionosphere was lifting, cooling under the stars. Arthur dimmed the oil lamp until the wick was just a red tooth glowing inside the soot-darkened chimney.

He closed his eyes.

Through the static, very faint, came a rhythmic scratching: three short, three long, three short, repeated not in the sharp, clipped cadence of a military key, but with the loose, wandering rhythm of a hand that was growing cold. It wasn't an emergency. It was simply an old circuit somewhere, perhaps a rusted buoy broken from its chain and drifting toward the Arctic pack, shorting out against the salt wash as it rolled in the trough of the dark waves.

Arthur didn't reach for the transmitter key. There was none to reach for; he had long since disconnected the lead. He simply listened, matching his breathing to the slow, stubborn pulse of the machine adrift in the dark, until the tape ran out of the spool with a soft, rhythmic *slap-slap-slap* against the deck, and the house was quiet again.
